title: Himyarite Kingdom
capsule: By the attested window (c. 534–578 CE) the independent Himyarite Kingdom of South Arabia had already ended: the Aksumite (Ethiopian) invasion of 525 had overthrown the Jewish king Yusuf As'ar Yath'ar (Dhu Nuwas), and Himyar was governed as a Christian dependency under Aksumite suzerainty. From about 535 the Aksumite general Abraha seized control of Himyar, deposing the viceroy Sumyafa Ashwa, resisting two punitive expeditions sent by King Kaleb of Aksum, and ruling as a largely autonomous Christian king of Himyar—commemorating his works in the Marib Dam inscription of 548 and reportedly mounting a campaign toward Mecca. After Abraha's death (by c. 570) his sons ruled briefly before a pro-Persian faction invited Sasanian intervention; between roughly 570 and 575 the general Wahriz expelled the Aksumites and brought Yemen under Sasanian Persian control.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The Himyarite Kingdom is attested through South Arabian inscriptions (Musnad script), Greek and Roman geographers, Syriac and Ethiopic hagiographic sources; core Yemeni territory is reasonably well documented, but the extent of nominal overlordship into central Arabia is based on inscriptional royal titulature rather than administered boundaries.
